title: Wash Rice Twice: UK Drought Campaign Targets South Asian Cooking Habits Amid Water Emergency
excerpt: England's water authorities are asking South Asian households to cut rice-washing from seven times to two and urging Muslims to reduce ablution water as more than half the country sits in drought.
body:
• England's water authorities are running targeted campaigns advising South Asian households to wash rice twice instead of the traditional seven times, and urging Muslims to perform wudu using a one-litre jug rather than a running tap.
  • The campaigns, funded by taxpayer money, come as more than half of England has been declared in drought following the driest July on record, with just 7 percent of expected rainfall.
  • Celebrity chef Ping Coombes is fronting the rice-washing campaign, advocating for reducing washes to save water during the crisis.
  • Seven water companies have imposed hosepipe bans affecting over 27 million customers, with one company seeking emergency non-essential use restrictions for the first time in two decades.

Drought Triggers Culturally Targeted Water Campaigns

As England endures its worst water crisis in nearly 50 years, government-backed campaigns are taking an unusual turn — directly targeting the cooking and religious practices of South Asian and Muslim communities to cut household water use.

The initiatives, backed by taxpayer funds, ask South Asian households to limit rice washing to twice instead of the traditional seven times. A parallel campaign urges Muslims to perform wudu — the ritual ablution before prayer — using a one-litre jug instead of running a tap, according to the Economic Times.

Malaysian-born celebrity chef Ping Coombes, a MasterChef winner, has been enlisted to front the rice-washing campaign. The approach reflects water authorities' recognition that blanket conservation messaging may not resonate equally across all communities, particularly those where water-intensive food preparation and religious practices are deeply embedded in daily life.

England's Water Emergency

The campaigns arrive amid what the Environment Agency has declared a "nationally significant" water crisis. More than half of England is officially in drought following what is set to be the driest July since records began in 1836, with just 7 percent of expected rainfall nationwide. Some parts of southern England received just 1 percent.

The drought has hit during England's fifth heatwave of 2026. Temperatures have repeatedly exceeded 30 degrees Celsius, with the Met Office recording 36 degrees in London — more than 15 degrees above the historical norm, according to Reuters' climate monitor. An estimated 2,877 people in Britain have died from heat-related causes this year.

Seven water companies have imposed temporary use bans — hosepipe bans — affecting more than 27 million customers. Southern Water, which serves Hampshire and the Isle of Wight, has applied for a non-essential use ban, a measure not invoked in two decades.

"The hot and dry weather means we are currently using water faster than nature can replenish it."

— Helen Wakeham, Director of Water, Environment Agency

Mixed Reactions From Diaspora Communities

The campaigns have drawn a mixed response. Supporters argue that culturally specific guidance is more effective than generic advice, noting that many South Asian families routinely wash rice five to seven times before cooking — a practice rooted in removing starch, impurities, and in some cases pesticide residues from grain.

Critics, however, question why cultural and religious practices are being singled out when agriculture and industrial leaks account for far larger shares of water consumption. England's ageing water infrastructure loses an estimated 3 billion litres daily to leaks, a figure that campaigners say dwarfs any savings from household behaviour changes.

The broader context adds another layer. The UK's water companies are privately owned, and several have faced public anger over sewage discharges, executive bonuses, and underinvestment in infrastructure — even as customers are asked to cut back.

A Deeper Climate Pattern

England's current drought is not an isolated event. The Environment Agency warned late last year that drought conditions from the record-breaking summer of 2025 were likely to persist into 2026 without significant winter rainfall. That rainfall never arrived in sufficient quantities.

The agency has estimated that without urgent conservation measures, England's public water supply could face a daily shortfall of 5 billion litres by 2055. Farmers have reported their earliest harvests in 20 years, with reduced crop yields and poor grass growth forcing livestock farmers to tap into winter forage stocks months ahead of schedule.

For the UK's South Asian communities — one of the country's largest ethnic minority groups — the campaigns raise uncomfortable questions about how conservation burdens are distributed. The underlying message is pragmatic: every litre counts during a genuine emergency. But the framing has reignited a familiar debate about whether individual behaviour change is being prioritized over systemic infrastructure failures.
